title: A pricing page for a manufacturer
metaTitle: What a manufacturer pricing page shows
excerpt: State what a price includes, what it excludes, and how quoting works. Buyers use this page to judge fit, then talk to sales or download a spec.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back, for a piece on showing both sides of a manufacturer's price.
caption: A product seen from the face and from the back. A price page should be that complete. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a manufacturer publish prices?
faqs.answer: Publish a number when it will still be true for the order a stranger is likely to place. When the figure depends on a drawing, publish the shape instead: what is included, what is excluded, how tooling is billed, and the minimum. Hiding even the shape forces the buyer to guess.

faqs.question: What belongs in the included list?
faqs.answer: The items a buyer would otherwise discover on the quote. Material, the primary operation, a standard finish, inspection, pack, and who owns the tool are typical. Samples and production should be distinguished if they are priced differently. Freight belongs in one plain line.

faqs.question: What is a minimum order doing on this page?
faqs.answer: Saving both sides a mismatched inquiry. If your floor is a quantity or a value, say so beside the pricing model. A buyer with a smaller need can decide before they write. Sales then spends time on work the shop can take.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A manufacturer pricing page helps a buyer who needs specs and confidence decide whether the commercial offer fits. Most of them are not there to finish a spreadsheet. They want the shape of the price: what is included, what is not, and how to talk to sales or download a spec. If they will ask anyway, the page should answer.

Print that shape even when the final figure depends on a drawing. "Quoted from your file, tooling separate, freight collected" is a shape. A button that says request a quote, with no sentence around it, sends the buyer away to guess. Guessing is how fit gets decided against you.

## Say the model before the table

Open with the way you sell. Catalog items at published prices. Configured products with a base and a list of adders. Fully custom work quoted from a drawing. Many shops are a mix. Say which product is which, in the first screen, in the words a buyer uses for those products.

A table can follow. It should not be the only explanation. A grid of numbers with no sentence about units is how a buyer misreads a per-piece price as a per-order price, or a setup fee as a unit cost. Label the unit. Piece, meter, hour, assembly, lot. Label the currency. Label whether tax and freight sit inside the figure.

If a number would be misleading without a volume, do not print a lonely "from" price that only exists at a quantity nobody orders. Either show the break, or describe the break in a sentence. "Unit price steps down at 100, 500, and 2,000" tells the truth without pretending every job has a shelf price.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page helps someone accomplish what they came to do, and whether the site has a clear purpose. On this page the purpose is a fit check. A buyer should leave knowing how you charge and what to do next. A page written to sound premium, with the commercial facts removed, fails that test.

## What the figure includes

List the inclusions as line items a purchasing manager can forward. Material, the primary operation, a standard finish, in-process checks, a standard pack. If first-article inspection, material certificates, or a control plan sit inside the quoted work, say so. If they are part of every order, they belong in the included list so they do not look like surprise adders later.

Tooling deserves its own sentence. Amortized into the unit price, billed once, or owned by the buyer and stored at the shop. Those are different deals. A founder who treats them as a detail will meet the objection in the first real conversation, after the buyer has already decided the website was vague.

Samples, prototypes, and production are different prices in most shops. If a sample is free above a volume, say the volume. If a sample is a paid first article, say that it is paid and what it proves. Buyers who need confidence use the sample path as a test of whether you are serious. Hide it and they assume the worst version.

Freight and incoterms can be one line. Ex-works, delivered to a dock, or collected by their forwarder. You do not need a lecture on trade terms. You need the buyer to know which of you arranges the truck. The same is true for export crates, certificates of origin, and who books the broker. If those are common in your orders, they are part of the shape.

## What the figure does not include

The exclusions are the half of the page that builds trust. Design help, CAD cleanup, custom fixtures beyond a standard setup, exotic material buys, expedited slots, on-site installation, and ongoing inventory holding. Name the ones that actually come up. A buyer who sees a clear outside edge can ask for it as an extra. A buyer who discovers it after the purchase order feels misled.

Write exclusions in the same tone as inclusions. They are boundaries. They are not a warning label. "We do not machine from a sketch with no dimensions" is a useful boundary. "Customer must ensure all requirements are communicated" is a shrug. The first tells an engineer how to show up. The second tells them the shop is preparing an excuse.

If a finish, a color match, or a secondary process is sometimes in and sometimes out, tie it to the product. Powder coat included on the outdoor line. Anodize quoted on the machined line. The page can hold two short lists. It cannot hold a paragraph that says everything depends.

## When the number itself should be public

Publish a number when it will still be true next month for the order a stranger is likely to place. Spare parts, stocked sizes, standard kits, and published setup fees often qualify. Custom geometry often does not. The failure is hiding a stable number because a competitor might see it. Your buyer will ask. A competitor who wants the number can ask too, or can already infer it.

When the number moves with metal markets, resin markets, or an energy surcharge, say how you update it. Monthly index, quote validity of a set number of days, or a surcharge line that is visible on the quote. You choose the rule that matches the shop. The page's job is to show that a rule exists.

Minimum order value and minimum quantity are part of the shape. A buyer with a five-piece need should learn that on the page if your floor is fifty. Letting them write a long inquiry and then hearing the floor on a call wastes their engineer and your sales desk. Put the floor next to the model.

Price breaks belong in the open when they are real. A sentence can do it when a full table would go stale. Keep the table when sales already sends the same table every week. The website should match the attachment your team already trusts.

## The spec and the sales path sit beside the price

A price without a spec is a number floating free of the object. Link the spec sheet, the standard drawing, or the configuration notes from the same screen as the price. The buyer who needs confidence is trying to see whether the included finish is the finish in the file. Make that check possible without a second hunt through the menu.

The next step matches the model. A catalog item can go toward an order or a sales conversation. A custom part should move toward a drawing upload or a talk with sales. Say what to have ready: file format, annual volume, material if they are specifying it, and the date they need parts. That list is the price page's form of respect. It tells a serious buyer you have done this before.

If the spec is the thing they came for, offer the download on this page too. Some buyers will never accept a public unit price, and they will still use the pricing page as a filter. Included, excluded, minimum, how quoting works, then the file. That path is enough for them to judge fit and take the next step.

Nielsen Norman Group's [study of how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that the average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and that people read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do see. The shape of the price has to live in the part they will actually reach. A long essay about partnership, with the minimum order in the footer, is a price page that fails in the first minute.

## Questions worth answering on the page

Read the last twenty quotes your team sent. The questions that appear in almost every thread belong on the page. Typical ones are setup, who owns the tool, how revisions are billed, what a change to a released drawing costs, and whether a blanket order holds a price. Answer the frequent ones in a few sentences each. Leave the rare ones for the call.

Keep the answers specific to your shop. A borrowed FAQ about "competitive pricing and dedicated support" answers nothing. "Drawing revisions after tool kickoff are quoted before we cut steel" answers something. The buyer can feel the difference immediately.

Say how long a quote usually takes only if you can keep the window. A published promise of same-day quotes, broken every week, is worse than silence. If engineering reviews drawings in the order they arrive and complex files take longer, say that. The point is a true expectation, tied to the work.

## Publish the page you can defend

Before the page goes up, a person who writes quotes should read it against a real quote. Every inclusion on the site should be an inclusion in the document. Every exclusion should be an exclusion they are willing to repeat on the phone. Where the site and the quote template disagree, fix one of them. Buyers notice the gap faster than internal reviewers do.

The visual design can be quiet. A clear stack of model, inclusions, exclusions, and the next step will do more than a pricing hero with a giant number you had to hedge in the caption. On a Hanabi project the page is built so those blocks can be edited when a standard changes, without a redesign of the whole site. The client portal can hold the current spec and the quote template next to the brand files, so sales and the site stay on the same revision.

If you want that page scoped with the rest of the marketing site, start from [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring a redacted quote and the spec you already send. The shape of the offer is usually already in those two files.

Once a buyer accepts the shape of the price, they look for the work itself, named the way they buy it. [The services page a manufacturer actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-manufacturer-actually-needs) is the next piece, because each capability still has to show an outcome, a boundary, and a way to talk to sales or take the spec.
